articles.title: Mandando Bem no Enem: psicólogo orienta cuidados na reta final da preparação | G1
articles.standfirst: Pedro Vittor Garcias Gonçalves, do Colégio Nacional, explica como organizar os estudos, lidar com o nervosismo e preservar o bem-estar antes da prova
articles.summary: Pedro Vittor Garcias Gonçalves, do Colégio Nacional, explica como organizar os estudos, lidar com o nervosismo e preservar o bem-estar antes da prova
articles.body:
Descanso, organização dos estudos e atenção aos próprios limites fazem parte da preparação para o Enem. — Foto: Imagem gerada por Inteligência Artificial.

Organizar os estudos e cuidar do bem-estar são partes da preparação para o Exame Nacional do Ensino Médio (Enem) 2026. Segundo Pedro Vittor Garcias Gonçalves, psicólogo escolar do Colégio Nacional (CRP 04/76334), a expectativa pelo resultado, a escolha profissional e as preocupações com o futuro podem tornar a reta final especialmente desafiadora.

“Sentir ansiedade, medo ou insegurança neste momento não significa estar despreparado”, afirma. Para o profissional, a tensão diante de uma situação importante não apaga o percurso de aulas, revisões e tentativas construído ao longo do ano.

Em vez de buscar eliminar completamente o nervosismo, a orientação é encontrar maneiras de lidar com ele sem deixar que tome conta da rotina. Descanso, alimentação, sono e lazer também precisam ter espaço nesse período.

Estude com estratégia e respeite seus limites

A vontade de revisar tudo pode aumentar a sensação de urgência. No entanto, tentar aprender todo o conteúdo desde o início em poucos dias pode gerar sobrecarga. Pedro recomenda priorizar revisões, resolução de questões e retomada dos assuntos já estudados. Os exercícios ajudam a identificar dúvidas e a ganhar familiaridade com o formato da prova.

Outro cuidado é considerar o tempo disponível e estabelecer uma organização realista. Dividir os estudos em blocos, alternando concentração e pequenas pausas, é uma possibilidade.

“Mais do que passar horas revisando, o objetivo é aproveitar melhor o tempo e reconhecer os próprios limites”, orienta o psicólogo.

O cuidado com o corpo também faz parte da preparação

A preparação também acontece fora dos momentos de estudo. Dormir bem contribui para a atenção e a memória, importantes tanto para aprender quanto para realizar a prova. Trocar noites de sono por horas extras de revisão pode prejudicar esse processo.

Manter uma alimentação variada e regular, beber água e incluir atividades físicas na rotina são outras formas de cuidado indicadas pelo profissional. A proposta não é fazer mudanças radicais, mas preservar pequenas escolhas consistentes que contribuam para o bem-estar.

O lazer também merece espaço. Encontrar amigos, ouvir música, assistir a um filme ou dedicar tempo a uma atividade de que se gosta não precisa ser motivo de culpa. Para Pedro, os interesses e as relações fazem parte do cuidado de si.

Evite medir sua preparação pelas redes sociais

Publicações sobre longas jornadas de estudo, listas de conteúdos revisados e resultados de simulados podem ampliar a impressão de que todos estão mais preparados. O psicólogo lembra que cada estudante tem uma trajetória, com oportunidades, dificuldades e ritmos diferentes.

O que aparece nas redes é um recorte da realidade de alguém. Em vez de usar esse conteúdo como medida do próprio desempenho, a orientação é reconhecer os avanços e identificar o que ainda pode ser feito dentro do tempo disponível.

Reorganize a atenção diante de uma questão difícil

No dia do Enem, além do conhecimento, fatores como cansaço e administração do tempo também entram em cena. Se uma questão parecer complicada, isso não significa que todo o desempenho esteja comprometido. Respirar com calma, reorganizar a atenção e seguir para outra questão são estratégias que podem ajudar a recuperar o foco.

“Nenhum exame resume o que um estudante é, aprendeu ou poderá construir no futuro”, ressalta Pedro. O Enem é uma etapa importante, mas não define a capacidade ou todas as possibilidades de quem participa.

A recomendação final é concentrar os esforços no que ainda está ao alcance, cuidar das condições que favorecem a aprendizagem e reconhecer o processo construído até aqui. Chegar à prova não exige saber absolutamente tudo, mas aproveitar o caminho percorrido e os recursos disponíveis.

articles.title: Mandando Bem no Enem: professores orientam o planejamento da redação | G1
articles.standfirst: Miriane Dayrell e Wagner Machado, do Colégio Nacional, mostram como organizar argumentos, usar repertório sociocultural e elaborar a proposta de intervenção
articles.summary: Miriane Dayrell e Wagner Machado, do Colégio Nacional, mostram como organizar argumentos, usar repertório sociocultural e elaborar a proposta de intervenção
articles.body:
Planejamento, repertório sociocultural e acompanhamento da escrita fazem parte da preparação para a redação do Enem — Foto: Imagem gerada por Inteligência Artificial

Ler a proposta, interpretar o tema e planejar os argumentos são etapas importantes para a redação do Exame Nacional do Ensino Médio (Enem) 2026. Segundo Miriane Dayrell e Wagner Machado, professores de Redação do Colégio Nacional, elaborar um projeto de texto ajuda o estudante a organizar conhecimentos e desenvolver uma argumentação consistente.

“Elaborar um projeto de texto demanda análise e articulação dos conhecimentos”, explicam.

Antes de escrever, a orientação é identificar o foco da frase temática. O estudante deve observar se a proposta pede uma discussão sobre desafios, caminhos, consequências ou estratégias, por exemplo. Essa leitura orienta a escolha do ponto de vista e dos argumentos que serão desenvolvidos.

Como forma de organizar a escrita, os professores sugerem uma introdução que apresente a situação-problema, a tese e os eixos da argumentação, seguida de dois parágrafos de desenvolvimento e de uma conclusão com proposta de intervenção.

No desenvolvimento, causas, consequências, dados e exemplos devem sustentar o ponto de vista apresentado. A organização precisa manter uma relação clara entre o que foi anunciado na introdução e o que será discutido ao longo da redação.

“Desde a introdução, é necessário destacar os pontos que serão desenvolvidos”, orientam.

Na conclusão, a proposta de intervenção deve estar relacionada ao problema discutido e apresentar agente, ação, meio de execução, finalidade e detalhamento. A orientação é indicar quem realizará a medida, o que será feito, como e com qual objetivo, detalhando um dos elementos. A proposta também deve respeitar os direitos humanos.

Segundo os professores, a articulação dos argumentos ajuda a construir intervenções com aplicabilidade social, conectadas às questões abordadas no texto.

Aulas de Ciências Humanas, filmes, séries, literatura e arte são fontes que podem contribuir para uma argumentação diversificada. Miriane e Wagner recomendam aproveitar essas experiências para relacionar conceitos, estabelecer analogias e analisar temas atuais.

“Um ponto essencial para desenvolver um bom texto: repertório sociocultural”, destacam.

A referência escolhida precisa ter uma relação com o tema e contribuir para o argumento. Para os professores, articular os conhecimentos dessa forma favorece a construção de textos originais e de análises que vão além de modelos previamente esquematizados.

Como a redação é trabalhada no Colégio Nacional

No Colégio Nacional, a preparação envolve aulas, correções e acompanhamento do desempenho individual. Em todas as séries do ensino médio, duas aulas seguidas são dedicadas ao estudo dos recursos argumentativos e à construção textual.

“Contamos com profissionais especializados na análise e correção dos textos, que ajudam cada estudante a reconhecer suas dificuldades e transformar os erros em oportunidades de aprendizado”, explicam.

O acompanhamento também utiliza gráficos e indicadores individuais para identificar avanços e pontos que precisam ser aprimorados. Segundo Miriane e Wagner, o objetivo é preparar os estudantes para produzir textos consistentes e bem estruturados por meio de um trabalho contínuo entre professores e alunos.

Os professores recomendam a leitura da Cartilha do Participante do Enem 2026, publicada pelo Instituto Nacional de Estudos e Pesquisas Educacionais Anísio Teixeira (Inep). O material apresenta orientações sobre a prova, os critérios de correção e exemplos de redações comentadas.

“Leia com atenção cada informação da cartilha. Além disso, aproveite para analisar as redações exemplares ao final do documento”, recomendam.

articles.title: ChatGPT vai limitar acesso de adolescentes a informações sobre armas | G1
articles.standfirst: Empresa também poderá suspender temporariamente contas após conversas recorrentes sobre violência e pretende reforçar alertas aos pais.
articles.summary: Empresa também poderá suspender temporariamente contas após conversas recorrentes sobre violência e pretende reforçar alertas aos pais.
articles.body:
ChatGPT — Foto: ANDREJ IVANOV / AFP via Getty Images

A OpenAI anunciou nesta sexta-feira (30) que vai restringir ainda mais as informações sobre armas fornecidas pelo ChatGPT a adolescentes, mesmo quando as perguntas parecerem inofensivas. A medida faz parte de novas ações de segurança para prevenir casos de violência no mundo real.

As novas regras também preveem que o ChatGPT possa encerrar automaticamente conversas quando identificar sinais de fixação em violência. Se isso ocorrer repetidas vezes, a OpenAI poderá suspender temporariamente a conta do usuário.

Entre as mudanças específicas para adolescentes, a empresa vai limitar o fornecimento de informações práticas sobre armas e sistemas de segurança que possam ser usadas de forma indevida, mesmo quando não houver sinais de intenção violenta.

Outra mudança envolve o sistema usado pela OpenAI para estimar a idade dos usuários. A empresa afirmou que aprimorou a tecnologia para direcionar à versão voltada a menores de 18 anos aqueles que o sistema identificar como adolescentes.

OpenAI também pretende notificar os pais que tenham suas contas vinculadas às dos filhos caso a conta do adolescente seja temporariamente suspensa por conversas recorrentes sobre violência.

Para todos os usuários, a empresa ainda vai reduzir o nível de detalhe fornecido sobre ataques em massa ocorridos no passado, incluindo informações sobre as armas utilizadas e como elas foram obtidas.

Segundo a OpenAI , as novas medidas de segurança começarão a ser implementadas nas próximas semanas e continuarão sendo aprimoradas.

As mudanças foram anunciadas em meio a discussões sobre a segurança de adolescentes que usam ferramentas de inteligência artificial.

No início deste mês, a OpenAI informou que esse público passa, em média, menos de 15 minutos por dia usando o ChatGPT . O dado consta do primeiro relatório da empresa sobre o uso do serviço por adolescentes.

Também neste mês, um relatório da organização sem fins lucrativos Common Sense Media apontou falhas nos alertas enviados aos pais pela versão do ChatGPT voltada a adolescentes.

Segundo a entidade, esses avisos frequentemente chegam tarde demais ou sequer são enviados quando adolescentes mantêm conversas sobre suicídio, automutilação ou transtornos alimentares.

articles.title: BRIAN HARRELL: America’s AI revolution can’t charge forward without lots of energy
articles.summary: Data centers demand massive electricity for AI, but who pays for the infrastructure? Why ratepayer protection and energy dominance matter now.
articles.body: The race for artificial intelligence (AI), or superintelligence, will be won not just by technology companies, but by the nation that can deliver reliable, affordable and secure electricity. America is in a high-stakes sprint to lead the world in AI. This technology will reshape our economy, strengthen national defense, transform manufacturing and determine which nations lead the next generation of innovation. But Washington and Silicon Valley cannot afford to ignore a glaring bottleneck: AI runs on electricity. America must dramatically expand its power generation and delivery infrastructure if it hopes to remain the global technology leader. Data centers are the backbone of this revolution. They require enormous amounts of electricity, reliable grid connections and specialized infrastructure. Without sufficient power, advanced AI systems are little more than expensive hardware waiting for a connection. This creates an immense opportunity for America’s electric utilities. For too long, utilities have been viewed simply as service providers. Today, they are strategic partners in America’s economic competitiveness and national security. THE AI REVOLUTION WILL GO WHEREVER THERE'S ELECTRICITY — AND CHINA KNOWS IT To win the AI race, America must unleash domestic energy production, accelerate infrastructure development, defend against cyber threats and ensure that the private sector — not residential ratepayers — finances this expansion. This is a crucial opportunity for the administration, Congress, state governments and the private sector to coordinate an energy strategy that prioritizes American competitiveness. Let the private sector finance growth Electric utilities possess the engineering expertise and operational experience necessary to support data center expansion. They understand regional demand, transmission constraints and the complex mechanics of grid reliability. However, building the necessary infrastructure takes time; new generation facilities, transmission lines and substations often require years of planning, permitting and construction. FIRST DATA CENTER BILL CLEARS HOUSE AS BOTH PARTIES SCRAMBLE FOR ANSWERS ON AFFORDABILITY Data center developers, meanwhile, want to move quickly to capitalize on the AI boom. To bridge this gap, utilities and developers must collaborate much earlier in the process, aligning construction schedules, forecasting demand and identifying necessary upfront investments. Washington can support this by streamlining permitting and reducing regulatory delays to provide long-term investment certainty. Crucially, data center developers must bear their fair share of the infrastructure costs driven by their massive electricity demands. Residential customers and small businesses should not subsidize infrastructure built primarily to serve trillion-dollar technology companies. Long-term power purchase agreements, dedicated infrastructure investments and minimum billing commitments can ensure large customers contribute appropriately. This is an argument for responsible, pro-business growth where financial risks are not shifted onto ordinary Americans. The White House’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge reinforces the principle that America can accelerate AI innovation without forcing ordinary Americans to subsidize Big Tech’s infrastructure demands. Electric utilities can benefit from increased electricity sales, long-term power contracts and investments in generation and grid infrastructure, provided data center developers pay their fair share of the costs. DATA CENTERS COULD BE THE SLEEPER ISSUE OF THE 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS To protect consumers, we must require transparent cost allocation, enforceable commitments from large data center customers and safeguards preventing residential ratepayers from being left with stranded infrastructure costs if projects are delayed, scaled back or abandoned. Energy dominance requires real abundance America cannot achieve energy dominance if it cannot generate enough electricity to power its expanding economy. Meeting this challenge requires an "all-of-the-above" strategy that evaluates energy resources strictly based on reliability, affordability and availability. TRUMP ENERGY DEPARTMENT ISSUES EMERGENCY ORDER TO PREVENT BLACKOUTS ACROSS 13 STATES AMID UNUSUAL OCTOBER HEAT Natural gas provides essential dispatchable generation, while nuclear energy offers dependable baseline power with low operational emissions. Hydroelectric power, wind, solar and battery storage all contribute where they make economic sense. Existing coal facilities also remain part of the equation where continued operation is economic and legally compliant. No single technology can solve every regional power challenge. Utilities need the flexibility to select the optimal resource mix for their customers. The objective is straightforward: build enough reliable generation and transmission capacity to meet rising demand without spiking energy prices. This is vital as data centers increasingly compete for power with manufacturers, hospitals, military bases and households. Energy abundance is a national security imperative. Securing the grid from cyber threats There is another critical threat that deserves far more attention: cybersecurity. The electric grid and digital infrastructure are deeply interconnected. Power disruptions halt essential computing services, while software incidents at technology providers can ripple back to affect critical infrastructure. Foreign adversaries and sophisticated cybercriminals understand these critical dependencies. America cannot achieve energy dominance if it cannot generate enough electricity to power its expanding economy. Electric utilities operate vital infrastructure that must withstand attacks against corporate networks, industrial control systems and substations. Concurrently, data centers face distinct risks involving cloud platforms, software supply chains and third-party vendor access. These are interconnected risks that could have significant national security consequences. AN AI CYBERATTACK COULD TURN OFF AMERICA'S LIGHTS BEFORE WASHINGTON EVEN UNDERSTANDS WHY Utilities and data center operators must establish joint incident response plans, conduct realistic multisector exercises and develop secure mechanisms for sharing threat intelligence. Organizations should strengthen network segmentation, multifactor authentication and vulnerability management. In particular, utilities must ensure that a compromise of ordinary corporate IT does not provide a path into operational technology controlling the grid. A stolen password should never become a gateway to disabling the power supply. Supply-chain security deserves equal focus. Hardware, software and remote maintenance arrangements can introduce vulnerabilities into both utility operations and data center environments. Companies must rigorously assess critical vendors and establish clear protocols for addressing compromised components. Security frameworks should remain risk-based, practical and focused on resilience. Data centers as grid assets The relationship between utilities and data centers should not be one-way. With the right investments, large computing facilities can help improve grid flexibility. Some AI training workloads can be shifted to off-peak hours, allowing operators to reduce consumption during periods of high demand. articles.title: Silicon Valley wants you to invest in miracles
articles.summary: Anthropic’s S-1 is a new milestone in Big Tech’s sprawling and lofty promises to Wall Street.
articles.body: Investing in any stock is kind of like gambling in the sense that you’re betting your money on a company’s future performance. But how do you bet on a technology that could, in the worst-case scenario, “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity,” or best case, “bring forth an age of miracles”? To some extent, Anthropic suggests in a letter at the top of its S-1 filing, you have to just believe. Anthropic’s 335-page S-1 prospectus, filed Monday, is part of a steady hype escalation in Silicon Valley’s interactions with Wall Street. In some ways, it’s not even that bizarre; SpaceX IPO’d in June after filing an S-1 that referenced dinosaurs and “colonizing Mars.” But its sweeping language and sheer volume — including 94 pages of risk factors — is a sometimes overwhelming collision of AI industry rhetoric and a hard financial pitch. Out-of-this-world promises are integral to Anthropic’s survival as a company. That doesn’t make reading the S-1 any less surreal. In the letter, Anthropic’s founders urge prospective stock owners “not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms. We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater.” The march toward advanced AI “is one of the seminal moments in human history,” the letter says. “Our aim is to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery, and bring forth an age of miracles.” But the S-1 warns that if things go wrong, the consequences could be disastrous — even an “existential” risk to humanity. Many dangers are laid out in exhaustive detail, including risks that models “behave in ways that no user or developer intended,” leading to “catastrophic” incidents that the entire insurance industry couldn’t afford to underwrite. Tech startups preparing to go public haven’t always used the information overload approach. “In 1980, a highly touted company called Apple Computer went public. Its prospectus, which I have, is 47 pages long with zero risk factors,” said Jay R. Ritter, a professor at the University of Florida’s Warrington College of Business. “If you go back and read it, it’s incredibly simple.” Ritter pointed to Facebook’s S-1 filing as a turning point. The company now known as Meta filed a 200-page prospectus with 22 pages of risk factors. CEO Mark Zuckerberg’s letter to investors was a manifesto on his move-fast-and-break-things approach to growth, which he dubbed “The Hacker Way.” While the idea might be to cover all possible bases, “a problem with this bloat is that it’s become more and more difficult to find the nuggets of what’s important,” Ritter said. “You know, I don’t know if you’re like me, but the longer it is, the less inclined I am to read it.” Anthropic’s founders explain in their investor letter that oversharing is part of their “anti-sell” strategy, designed to attract long-term investors who believe in their vision. “It is very dangerous when people buy your company’s stock based on expectations you cannot fulfill or on incorrect predictions about how you will behave. This is in fact very similar to one of Anthropic’s guiding principles: underpromise and overdeliver,” the founders’ letter says. Some of the statements in Anthropic’s S-1 read as surprising admissions. “We may make forward investments that may seem irresponsibly large,” for instance, or “model safety, interpretability, alignment, and welfare may lead us to limit or delay the deprecation of older models.” Maybe none of this should be surprising, considering the founders do warn readers about the company’s policy of practicing “radical honesty.” This policy led to the biggest jumpscare of the whole filing, on page 46: “Concerns have been raised both within our organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants that, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” Followed quickly by: “Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could further increase the risk that our models cause harm.” Anthropic has famously been a proponent of doomsday AI scenarios. CEO Dario Amodei has said there’s an up to 25 percent chance that further AI development could lead to human extinction. The heart of Anthropic’s pitch — or anti-sell — is that despite the risks, it is absolutely committed to developing safe and secure AI technology. After all, it will go public as a public benefit corporation, a type of business entity that, unlike C-corporations that are required to maximize shareholder value, must prioritize a social mission alongside shareholder interests. “Powerful AI” — Anthropic’s term for hypothetical future AI that surpasses collective human intelligence — is presented in the company’s S-1 as inevitable. If this technology is coming no matter what, then Anthropic, a public benefit corporation, should lead the charge. But Anthropic will need a lot of money, possibly an unlimited amount, to do this. And more practically, as Liz Lopatto has written, powerful AI (in the form of dramatic recursive self-improvement) might be about the only way Anthropic can stay ahead of the competition and survive. “All of us have a sincere conviction that the AI exponential will generate so much value, that, in the long run, it will far outweigh any shorter-term economic sacrifices we make as part of our mission,” the letter says. For all the information the company made available in its S-1, there are some gaps. Crucial information that could be used to assess profitability — third quarter results, for instance — is missing. Anthropic saw explosive revenue growth in the second quarter, but the second quarter was also the height of tokenmaxxing, which could have led to a surge in sales. Some corporate executives have warned that AI costs are surging out of control. While Anthropic’s operating losses narrowed in the second quarter, the S-1 also revealed hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations to secure the computing power it says it needs to keep growing. It also said it will start building its own data center infrastructure, a costly move that would eat into profit. Ritter thinks Anthropic will likely share its third quarter results the closer it gets to an IPO date. And besides, he added, “nobody knows” what will happen once a company goes public, including the company itself. It’s all a gamble in that sense. “For its first 22 years, Apple was largely a failure as far as investors were concerned,” Ritter said. “In its first three years, it greatly underperformed the market. And now it’s worth what, $5 trillion?” When WeWork filed its S-1 in 2019, it was skewered for using lofty rhetoric. A line about the company’s aim to “elevate the world’s consciousness” was especially roasted. That was different, Ritter said. WeWork was “a money-losing real estate company pretending to be a tech company at a ridiculously high valuation.” “There was no chance of ever making huge profits in the future.” Technically, that’s a risk for Anthropic too. It’s on page 63 of the S-1. “We have a history of net losses and may not generate sufficient revenue to achieve or sustain profitability in the future.” Then again, this is the age of miracles.

articles.title: DoorDash said it’s only received ‘several hundred’ orders from AI agents
articles.summary: DoorDash said that it is open to working with third-party agent makers.
articles.body:
There’s a big uproar about AI agents taking over commerce and orders, but that might not be the case just yet. Delivery company DoorDash revealed during its third-quarter earnings call that it has only seen “several hundred” orders from third-party agents like Muse, Instinct, Fo, and others. For comparison, the company said in its 2025 report it completes an average of 3 million deliveries daily.

“I would say that this [using agents to order] is something that is still a very dynamic area. And my take on all things technology is you never want to fight gravity. But at the same time, you don’t want to be delusional,” DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said in an answer to an analyst’s questions about the topic. “What I mean by that is if you look at where AI agents are today, we’re seeing maybe several hundred orders in total from some of these third-party agents,” he said.

Xu mentioned that users are still predominantly placing orders through DoorDash’s app. However, the company wants to learn more about agentic use cases and develop a healthy relationship with third-party agent makers. He added that, in the future, there could be an opportunity for it to advertise within these agents.

DoorDash has its own agents, including a text-to-order agent it launched in September , a CLI agent introduced in July , and a chatbot called Ask DoorDash it launched in June, which allows users to place orders through prompts and photos . The company also released an MCP to enable ordering from other chatbots for corporate ordering.

The space of agent-based ordering is evolving, as websites are still deciding whether to allow them to access their content or not. Amazon has been blocking such personal agents, but Walmart has laid out a red carpet for them in order to snag some business from its competitors .

For comparison, the company said in its 2025 report it completes an average of 3 million deliveries daily.

"I would say that this [using agents to order] is something that is still a very dynamic area. And my take on all things technology is you never want to fight gravity. But at the same time, you don't want to be delusional," DoorDash CEO Tony Xu said in an answer to an analyst's questions about the topic. "What I mean by that is if you look at where AI agents are today, we're seeing maybe several hundred orders in total from some of these third-party agents," he said.

Xu mentioned that users are still predominantly placing orders through DoorDash's app. However, the company wants to learn more about agentic use cases and develop a healthy relationship with third-party agent makers. He added that, in the future, there could be an opportunity for it to advertise within these agents.

DoorDash has its own agents, including a text-to-order agent it launched in September , a CLI agent introduced in July , and a chatbot called Ask DoorDash it launched in June, which allows users to place orders through prompts and photos . The company also released an MCP to enable ordering from other chatbots for corporate ordering.

The space of agent-based ordering is evolving, as websites are still deciding whether to allow them to access their content or not. Amazon has been blocking such personal agents, but Walmart has laid out a red carpet for them in order to snag some business from its competitors .

articles.title: AI-powered cyberattacks fuel 'Black October' fears
articles.summary: A startup founder woke to $449 in unexpected OpenAI and Anthropic charges after stolen API keys were exploited during the "Black October" cyber wave.
articles.body: Startup founder Colin Parsons woke up to roughly 50 billing notifications he never expected. He reported that his OpenAI and Anthropic accounts had racked up $449 in charges he didn't recognize. It was an expensive surprise that highlights how quickly stolen credentials can become a financial headache. His experience comes as hackers increasingly use artificial intelligence to automate attacks at speeds that leave security teams scrambling. Meanwhile, researchers have uncovered dangerous weaknesses in software that helps power millions of websites. Some cybersecurity professionals are calling this turbulent period "Black October." The name may sound dramatic, but the developments behind it deserve attention. And while many attacks target large organizations, the consequences can eventually reach your personal accounts. Here's what's happening, how AI-powered cyberattacks are changing online security and what you can do to protect yourself. Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com. BILL GATES SOUNDS ALARM ON AI-POWERED CYBERATTACKS, WARNS OF 'NEGATIVE SURPRISES' WITHIN A YEAR Why cybersecurity experts are calling it Black October October 2026 has delivered a troubling wave of cybersecurity developments. Hackers have gained access to more powerful tools, while researchers have uncovered serious weaknesses in widely used software. Security professionals are reportedly struggling to keep pace with increasingly automated attacks. Some have started calling the current wave "Black October." The term describes a series of cybersecurity emergencies rather than a single coordinated hacking campaign. The biggest concern is speed. Traditionally, hackers needed significant time and technical expertise to investigate potential targets. They also had to develop attack methods and analyze the information they obtained. Now, AI tools can automate portions of that work. Some can operate continuously and pursue multiple potential targets at once. As a result, companies may have less time to respond when criminals discover a way into their systems. Microsoft exposes AI cyberattacks moving at machine speed One of the clearest examples comes from Microsoft. On Oct. 21, Microsoft Threat Intelligence revealed that a China-state-aligned hacking group called Storm-0940 had used an AI-powered penetration testing framework called ARTEX. The open-source tool can automate security testing tasks, including investigating networks and identifying potential weaknesses. In the hands of criminals, those capabilities can accelerate attempts to gain unauthorized access. According to Microsoft, the group used ARTEX to target hundreds of organizations across multiple industries. Several attacks resulted in unauthorized privileged access to cloud systems. In multiple cases, attackers reached that level of access in less than three hours. Although many attempts failed, the successful intrusions demonstrate how quickly AI-assisted attacks can unfold. Hackers launch thousands of login attempts per minute Between Oct. 10 and 14, Microsoft recorded more than 151,000 failed login attempts in one campaign targeting 327 accounts across eight organizations. At its peak on Oct. 11, attackers generated approximately 2,900 failed login attempts per minute. The technique, known as password spraying, involves trying passwords against multiple accounts to identify a working login. Importantly, Microsoft did not observe successful logins during that specific campaign. However, it documented unauthorized access and suspicious activity in other environments associated with the same threat group. Microsoft also connected Storm-0940 to a compromise involving ConnectWise, a company that provides software used by IT service providers. Attackers exploited access associated with ConnectWise cloud applications to attempt entry into customer environments. Some then carried out further activity through Microsoft cloud services, including changes that could help them maintain access. Microsoft cautioned that suspicious access does not automatically mean customer information was stolen. Nevertheless, the activity reveals how AI can help attackers move quickly once they obtain usable credentials. A $449 AI account scare shows the financial danger The risks become more personal when you look at what happened to Colin Parsons. Parsons reportedly woke up to roughly 50 notifications about charges involving OpenAI and Anthropic. He reported $281 in unexpected OpenAI usage and another $168 involving Anthropic. Both credentials were associated with OpenCode, an AI coding platform he used. On Oct. 17, OpenCode disclosed a security incident involving its Console service. The company said unauthorized access to a legacy system may have exposed third-party AI provider keys stored by some users. The company reportedly notified affected customers and advised them to revoke their credentials. OpenCode said the incident affected approximately 1.4% of its Console users who had connected external AI providers. The disclosure concerned credentials stored in Console, rather than keys stored locally in OpenCode's desktop or command-line applications. Other users also reported unexpected charges, although the amounts have not been independently verified. OpenCode associated its incident with a large-scale AI model distillation attack, but it has not publicly established exactly how the reported unauthorized usage occurred. The concern is straightforward. If someone obtains a working API key, they may be able to use a paid AI service and generate charges against the account owner's billing arrangement. For people who depend on AI tools for work, that can become expensive before they realize anything has happened. WINDOWS MALWARE USES GROK AI TO HELP STAY HIDDEN, RESEARCHERS SAY A massive website security scare adds to Black October fears While hackers are becoming more capable, AI-assisted security research is also uncovering dangerous weaknesses in software that supports the internet. On Oct. 21, developers released emergency fixes for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a programming language widely used to operate websites. The vulnerabilities, identified as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, are collectively known as PHP2Shell. Under certain conditions, the flaws could allow attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers without first signing in. Successful exploitation could expose sensitive information or give criminals control over affected systems. The potential impact is enormous because PHP powers roughly 70% of websites whose server-side programming language is known. However, that does not mean 70% of websites were hacked. It also doesn't establish that attackers could successfully compromise every website using PHP. The vulnerabilities affect PHP installations handling web requests, but successfully exploiting them can require complex technical conditions. Federal agencies issue urgent security warnings The situation prompted warnings from U.S. cybersecurity authorities. On Oct. 23, the FBI issued a public alert urging organizations to patch affected systems immediately. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency also called for urgent updates. The PHP project released fixes in versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. Website administrators running older unsupported versions need to obtain appropriate vendor-supported fixes or migrate to a supported release. Meanwhile, several government organizations in Europe temporarily took websites offline as a precaution. However, the situation became clearer as researchers investigated. On Oct. 23, the Netherlands' National Cyber Security Centre said exploiting the vulnerabilities appeared more complicated than initially feared. The agency lowered its assessment of the likelihood of widespread exploitation. Also on Oct. 23, PHP disclosed a separate vulnerability, CVE-2026-115560, involving an unusual combination of server settings and application code. The project recommended a temporary configuration change while it prepares a fix through its regular release process. Website owners should continue following official PHP security guidance rather than assuming the emergency has completely passed. Cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike also reported seeing attempted attacks, but said it had not observed successful exploitation of PHP2Shell in its investigations at that point. Other security researchers, including Amazon Threat Intelligence, observed suspicious exploitation attempts beginning before the patches became publicly available. Those attempts remain important even without proof that they successfully compromised real systems. However, new evidence emerged over the following days. On Oct. 24, security researcher Adel Karimi documented successful PHP2Shell exploitation against specially configured test servers, known as honeypots. The attacks launched 35 command shells across three honeypots. Although those findings did not establish how many real-world websites had been compromised, they demonstrated that attackers could successfully exploit the vulnerability under certain conditions. Then, on Oct. 26, CISA added both PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The designation confirms that federal authorities recognize evidence of active exploitation. It also reinforces the urgency of installing security updates, even though the full extent of attacks against real-world systems remains unclear. AI is helping hackers, but security researchers are using it too There's another side to this story that deserves attention. Artificial intelligence helped researchers investigate the PHP vulnerabilities before the October emergency. According to the PHP Foundation, developers had identified early signs of one underlying problem during a security investigation in 2024. However, the team struggled to develop a reliable solution. Additional research in 2026 exposed the seriousness of the issue. The foundation worked with researchers and used AI-assisted security tools, including technology from Anthropic and OpenAI, to examine PHP's code. Researchers from security companies Calif and Wiz also contributed important findings. The PHP Foundation says these reports helped clarify the vulnerabilities' potential impact and accelerated the work needed to release fixes. AI can therefore help defenders identify dangerous weaknesses before criminals exploit them. The challenge is ensuring security teams can investigate the findings and distribute fixes quickly enough. That challenge is becoming more urgent. What AI-powered cyberattacks mean for your personal information You may be wondering how any of this affects you if you're simply checking email or shopping online. The concern starts with the companies holding your information. When hackers compromise a business, they may gain access to stored customer information. Depending on the systems involved, that could include email addresses or passwords. Financial details may also be exposed. Criminals can use stolen information to launch convincing scams or attempt to take over existing accounts. Meanwhile, AI makes it easier to produce personalized phishing messages. Attackers can incorporate leaked information into emails that appear to come from a company you recognize. Some criminals also use AI-generated voices to impersonate people and pressure their targets into making payments. However, a security vulnerability affecting a website doesn't automatically mean your personal information has been exposed. The actual risk depends on whether attackers successfully gained access and what information they obtained. That's why it helps to focus on the steps you can control. HACKERS HIDE DANGEROUS FAKE AI DOWNLOADS BEHIND GOOGLE ADS 8 ways to protect yourself from AI-powered cyberattacks You can't personally fix security problems affecting large companies. However, you can strengthen your accounts and reduce the potential damage if criminals obtain your information. Here are seven precautions I recommend taking now. 1. Secure your most important accounts first Start with your primary email account. Criminals who gain access to it may be able to reset passwords for other services you use. Create a strong, unique password for every account. A reputable password manager can help you generate and store those passwords. Next, enable multifactor authentication wherever it's available. Passkeys and hardware security keys offer especially strong protection against phishing. Authenticator apps are another useful option. Avoid relying on passwords alone. 2. Check whether your passwords have been compromised Your phone may already have tools that can identify passwords exposed in known data breaches. On an iPhone, open the Passwords app and review its Security section. Android users who save passwords through Google can review warnings in Google Password Manager. If a password has been exposed, change it directly through the company's official website or app. Also update any other accounts using that same password. Our article explains how to find compromised passwords on iPhone and Android. Remember, a compromised-password warning does not necessarily mean someone has accessed your account. However, it gives you a chance to replace a vulnerable login. 3. Watch your accounts for suspicious activity Enable transaction notifications through your bank and credit card providers. Also review recent sign-ins on your email accounts and other important services. Watch for unfamiliar devices or changes to your recovery information. If you spot unauthorized activity, contact the provider through its official website or app. Change affected credentials and revoke unfamiliar sessions where possible. Don't wait for several suspicious charges before investigating. 4. Review which apps can access your information Many people connect third-party apps to their Google or Microsoft accounts without thinking about the permissions they're granting. Over time, those connections can accumulate. Some applications may retain access even after you've stopped using them. Open your account's security settings and review connected applications. Remove access you no longer need or recognize. However, if a service you use has announced a security incident, follow its specific recovery instructions. Simply disconnecting an app may not revoke credentials that attackers already obtained. 5. Use strong security protection and monitor your identity Strong antivirus software can help detect malicious downloads and block dangerous websites. However, antivirus protection cannot prevent every account takeover or stop a company from experiencing a data breach. That's why monitoring your financial information is also important. Consider placing a free credit freeze with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion to help prevent criminals from opening new credit accounts in your name. Keep in mind that a freeze won't protect accounts you already have. If you use AI services that require API keys, review your usage regularly. Revoke credentials that may have been exposed and set billing alerts or limits where the provider supports them. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. 6. Consider using a personal data removal service Data brokers collect and sell personal information, including phone numbers and home addresses. Criminals can use those details to make AI-generated scams more convincing. A personal data removal service can help remove your information from people-search sites and data broker databases, making it harder for scammers to find. However, it can't erase information from past breaches or prevent cyberattacks. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com. 7. Keep your devices and software updated Enable automatic security updates on your phone and computer. Keep your browser current, too. Updates frequently fix vulnerabilities that criminals may try to exploit. 8. Be skeptical of urgent security messages AI-generated phishing messages can look remarkably convincing. They may contain personal information that makes them appear legitimate. Be cautious if someone unexpectedly claims your account has been compromised or demands immediate payment. Instead of clicking a link, open the company's official app or visit its website directly. Never share a verification code with someone who contacts you unexpectedly. Criminals often create pressure because they want you to act before checking the details. Kurt's key takeaways What concerns me most about this wave of AI-powered cyberattacks is the speed. Microsoft documented attackers gaining privileged access in less than three hours. That's a frighteningly short window for companies to react. At the same time, AI is helping security researchers uncover weaknesses before criminals exploit them. But here's what worries me. We trust companies with enormous amounts of personal information, yet we're often left dealing with the fallout when their security fails. I believe those companies need to be held more accountable. Until then, protecting our accounts and staying alert to suspicious activity remains our best defense. If AI allows hackers to attack thousands of accounts in minutes, should companies face tougher penalties when they fail to protect our personal information? articles.title: Pope Leo calls for the disarmament of AI: ‘Machines are tools, not persons’
articles.summary: Pope Leo says AI systems should be “disarmed,” adding that UN member states should take steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.
articles.body: Pope Leo XIV says AI systems should be “disarmed,” adding that humans “have the responsibility to guide, change and, when necessary, reject its applications.” In Friday’s Papal Address, Pope Leo encourages United Nations member states to “take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons” during their meeting in Geneva next month. The address reflects many of the ideas Pope Leo laid out in his first major papal document in May, which highlighted “safeguarding the human person in the time of artificial intelligence.” In line with his encyclical, Pope Leo tells participants that “Machines are tools, not persons,” and warns about the dangers of granting AI systems rights or legal personhood. “Decisions affecting human life, freedom, and the use of force must always remain subject to effective, informed, and responsible human oversight,” Pope Leo says. In 2024, Pope Francis similarly called for a ban on autonomous weapons, saying, “No machine should ever choose to take the life of a human being.” AI has become a popular topic for Pope Leo, who suggests he chose his name because he must confront advances in the technology — similar to how Pope Leo XIII presided over the church at the forefront of the Industrial Revolution. Pope Leo closes out his address by calling for international institutions to safeguard the common good from AI-related risks, along with “shared standards, independent oversight and clear mechanisms of accountability so that decisions concerning the development and use of AI can be examined, challenged when necessary, and accompanied by appropriate remedies for any harm caused.”

articles.title: Theranos whistleblower Tyler Shultz warns that the AI boom is 'a great opportunity to go deceive people' | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The cautionary Theranos tale takes on a new significance in the AI era, when companies that have never turned a profit are raising capital at trillion-dollar valuations.
articles.body:
“ You Can See Everything ,” the documentary capturing disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes’ final weeks before prison, is sparking national conversation as it becomes one of the highest-grossing documentaries of all time. The film, directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, intentionally refuses to characterize Holmes as a master manipulator or victim, instead highlighting her uncanny, almost hypnotic knack for making people pity her, even when they’re well aware of her crimes .

Tyler Shultz didn’t need to see “You Can See Everything” to make up his mind about Holmes. Shultz, whose first job out of college was at Theranos, was a key whistleblower who exposed the company’s dangerously inaccurate blood testing devices, which made their way into Walgreens stores and delivered faulty results to real patients. (Theranos reached a peak valuation of around $10 billion despite its technology never actually working — the company only used its own machines for a fraction of tests , instead outsourcing others to third-party equipment.)

There is little reason to keep talking about Holmes — her case is closed, and she’s in federal prison — but her con-artistry has fascinated the media ( myself included ) for the last decade.

In fact, as Shultz says in an interview with The San Francisco Standard, “the only reason we’re talking about Elizabeth Holmes right now is because she wants us to be talking about Elizabeth Holmes right now.”

But the cautionary tale of Theranos takes on a new significance as we enter the peak of the AI era, when companies that have never turned a profit are raising capital at trillion-dollar valuations.

“I think the days of having a thirty-minute coffee with someone and sending them $100,000 should be over. Elizabeth took that model and scaled it to $100 million,” Shultz told SF Standard .

His grandfather, former U.S. Secretary of State and Secretary of the Treasury George Shultz, was a notable investor and board member himself.

“I believe that what [Holmes] did was raise the biggest angel round of funding of all time, but even at the smaller levels, I think investors need to recognize that when they put that type of money in someone’s hands, they are giving them tremendous power,” he added.

Theranos’ funding often came from individual investors like the DeVos and Walton families, rather than venture firms. Theranos did not share scientific information or evidence that its machines worked with potential investors, citing concerns about revealing trade secrets, which warded off many top venture capitalists in Silicon Valley.

At the time Theranos’ fraud was uncovered, it was seen as a shrill wake-up call for investors that they need to prioritize due diligence. But in the AI era, Shultz worries that investors may forget these lessons.

“A huge danger with AI is that I think it is really hard to do due diligence on it,” he said. “It’s really hard to tell the difference between what is something truly unique and new versus like, a ChatGPT wrapper… If you want to deceive people, I think this is a great opportunity to go deceive people.”

The first question posed by “You Can See Everything” lies in the premise of the movie itself. Why would a mother of two young children choose to invite a film crew to follow her final days with her family before surrendering to serve a prison sentence of over 11 years? The film poses questions that seem inscrutable, but this one seems pretty clear. She wants people to pity her, because this pity could be more useful for her future endeavors than hate or mockery.

In the film, we see Holmes and her partner, hotel heir Billy Evans, working on Haemanthus , a diagnostics company that they call “Theranos 2.0,” which has reportedly raised about $20 million in funding.

“You Can See Everything” doesn’t make Holmes look good, but it also glosses over the more heinous crimes of Theranos, like giving dangerously faulty medical information to real patients, or even its targeted harassment of Shultz himself when he was attempting to sound the alarm about his former employer. In the cultural zeitgeist, Holmes remains more of a joke than a persona non grata.

“I have this feeling of unease about what might come next,” Shultz said. “She’s certainly preparing and beginning her second act, and I don’t know exactly where it’s going to go.”

articles.title: Amazon Taps $80 Billion Supplier Loan Facility to Help Fund AI
articles.summary: Amazon.com Inc. has set up supplier financing arrangements to borrow as much as $80 billion against the value of hardware it buys, the company’s latest move...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Amazon.com Inc. has set up supplier financing arrangements to borrow as much as $80 billion against the value of hardware it buys, the company's latest move to preserve financial flexibility as it spends hundreds of billions on artificial intelligence infrastructure.

Amazon has so far funded data center construction and purchases of chips with the cash from its cloud-computing and retail operations, and with its biggest-ever corporate bond sales.

But it had largely avoided the sort of creative funding arrangements used by some of its rivals, including deals with investment groups to jointly finance data center construction or to lease chips purchased by other entities. Many of those deals have focused on the Nvidia Corp. chips that power most AI work and are often the single most expensive component of new data center construction.

The secured loan facility, which Amazon disclosed in a quarterly filing after reporting earnings on Thursday, can be tapped at the company's discretion from the beginning of 2027 through the third quarter of 2028. Lenders will get collateral rights over some of the assets purchased in connection with the facility. Amazon's filing doesn't specify what those assets included, and a spokesperson declined to comment.

"When we see such a really large opportunity in front of us, we're looking for ways to also responsibly fund that so that we can go as big as possible for our customers," Amazon Web Services Chief Executive Officer Matt Garman said in an interview on Bloomberg Television on Friday. Amazon, he said, was working with partners to "figure out how we can balance some of those cash flows as we're really ramping up aggressively."

On Thursday, Amazon reported a larger-than-expected increase in capital spending in its third-quarter earnings. The outlays led to a free cash outflow of $42.4 billion during the year ended Sept. 30. The shares were down about 2% at midday in New York.

Amazon's total spending commitments — including debt and interest, leases not yet commenced, obligations to acquire property and equipment and other line items — ballooned to $883 billion at the end of September, up 36% from three months earlier and more than double where that figure stood at the same point in 2025.

articles.title: Google’s first data center satellite is online and writing poetry
articles.summary: The first TPU in space is running a Google DeepMind Gemma 4 model and writing cheesy poetry.
articles.body:
Google Suncatcher’s prototype space data center is online and communicating with the ground after launching earlier this month alongside more than 100 other spacecraft on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket.

The satellite, which carries four Google Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) and generates up to 1 kW of electricity, is intended to pave the way for future networks of close-flying satellites performing large inference workloads in orbit. However, the power demands of the TPU mean it can only turn one on for about 20 minutes at a time, complicating the already tricky business of space-to-ground communications.

After a commissioning process that tested out the satellite’s subsystems over about three weeks, the spacecraft was ready to work. When engineers on the ground sent their first prompt this week, they asked the model pre-loaded onto the satellite, Google DeepMind’s Gemma 4, to write a haiku about being in space. And thus:

Blue marble below Data streams in silent grace Starlight feeds my core. ✨

Google said it tested the model with these space-themed limericks (they should have sent a poet?) and, perhaps more importantly, the company asked the spacecraft to report on the orbital conditions around the satellite.

A spokesperson told TechCrunch that the satellite was operating nominally.

The ongoing test campaign will examine how the chips perform under thermal stress and in the space radiation environment. Google has extensively tested its TPUs in particle accelerators on Earth, but now needs to see how radiation’s real effects on their hardware in space affect their processor. Radiation can cause “bit flips” — causing a stored value in computer memory — and that in turn can corrupt data without triggering typical monitoring tools.

Testing on the ground suggested the impact of radiation would be minimal for inference workloads and more of a problem for training a model, but now the Google team will get to assess those dynamics in reality, not a simulation.

If the TPUs onboard this spacecraft prove capable, the next step will be launching two more satellites equipped with the advanced chips in 2027. Those spacecraft will support higher power generation and demonstrate inter-satellite optical links.

Google’s Suncatcher project is largely alone among visions for space-based data centers in planning on high-speed links between the satellites to support coherent distributed workloads; SpaceX’s data centers are also expected to use laser links but also to orbit too far apart to share processing effectively. Companies like Starcloud and Cowboy Space expect to perform inference loads on individual satellites.

Google and SpaceX’s visions are closely linked. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, holds a significant investment stake in SpaceX. And to launch their orbital data centers, both companies will require Starship, the still-in-development heavy-lift rocket at the center of Elon Musk’s space vision, to be fully and rapidly reusable.

In a peer-reviewed analysis published earlier this month, Suncatcher researchers estimated that SpaceX would need to fly Starship 1,800 times to achieve the same learning-driven cost reductions it saw with its earlier vehicles. Suncatcher is a classic Google moonshot — the company’s focus is on designing infrastructure that will be economical in the 2030s. Getting there, however, may depend on how the rest of the company responds to the pressures and opportunities of AI in the near term. Alphabet, Google’s parent company, saw its stock plunge this week after reporting that efforts to insert AI into its search businesses are hurting ad revenue growth.

Correction: The Suncatcher prototype satellite has four TPUs onboard, but can only operate one at a time.

articles.title: Starbucks wants to use AI to show you a ‘personalized digital menu’ at the drive-thru
articles.summary: Starbucks is looking into personalized digital menu boards that change when a participating customer arrives at the drive-thru.
articles.body: Starbucks could eventually show you a personalized digital menu when you pull up to the drive-thru. During an earnings call on Thursday, Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol said the company is going to explore “experiences that recognize participating customers as they arrive, present personalized digital menus, and make payment more effortless,” as spotted earlier by More Perfect Union. It sounds similar to the technology that Taco Bell is experimenting with, which could change the layout, content, and visuals on a digital menu board “on a car-by-car basis.” McDonald’s also recently showed off an AI-powered feature it’s piloting at a handful of drive-thrus, allowing its “ArchIQ” chatbot to identify repeat customers and let them order their “usual.” Starting in 2027, Starbucks will also begin testing background AI models at the drive-thru to help baristas “input orders more accurately and efficiently,” according to Niccol. The company also plans to integrate AI into the Starbucks app’s search and discovery features, and may allow “conversational and agentic” ordering in the future. Starbucks has already started allowing customers to place orders through ChatGPT, and also rolled out an AI-powered Green Dot Assist that employees can use to ask questions about things like recipes and service standards. It’s still not clear how soon we can expect to see personalized digital menu boards at Starbucks, but Niccol says it’s still “early,” adding that “we’ll test, learn, and scale what works.”

articles.title: Fox News AI Newsletter: Don't want AI on your phone? What to do about it
articles.summary: The Fox News AI Newsletter covers the latest artificial intelligence technology advancements, including the challenges and opportunities AI presents now and for the future.
articles.body: Welcome to Fox News’ Artificial Intelligence newsletter with the latest AI technology advancements. IN TODAY’S NEWSLETTER: - How to get rid of unwanted AI on your phone - Microsoft offers voluntary buyouts to 60,000 employees as tech giant reshapes its workforce - Anthropic discloses breaches, security-related training pause in IPO filing OPTING OUT: You pull out your phone to look something up on Google. Maybe you're researching a purchase or trying to find a restaurant. You expect a list of websites. articles.title: Unvetted foreign workers at AI firms raise national security alarms, advocates warn
articles.summary: Tech advocacy groups warn that foreign nationals at AI companies like OpenAI and Google pose a national security threat amid a lack of federal oversight.
articles.body: Tech advocacy groups are sounding the alarm, warning that the rapid evolution of artificial intelligence and a lack of federal oversight for foreign nationals working at AI firms pose a major national security risk. Amy Kremer, chair of Humans First, a group focused on establishing democratic oversight, safety protocols, and local control over artificial intelligence, said AI technology has virtually no federal guardrails compared to other tech sectors. "This is a national security threat. These companies hold and have access to a lot of sensitive information," Kremer told Fox News Digital. "You don't have to steal an entire AI model to get information. You can just find out what they're working on, who their partners are, and who their adversaries are. That is not the kind of thing that we need getting out." MAGA MOM'S DIRE WARNING OVER TECH GUARDRAILS AS TRUMP PUTS PEDAL TO THE METAL ON RACE WITH CHINA "If America wants to lead the world on AI, and we want America to have this AI advantage, then we have to put national security at the top," she added. Kremer's concerns come as AI continues to expand, even as many Americans and lawmakers remain wary of the fast-moving industry. WATCH: AI SAFETY SCARE SPARKS CAP HILL FIGHT OVER GUARDRAILS: 'CHINA'S GOING TO EAT OUR LUNCH' In early October, an engineer at OpenAI, one of the world's most prominent AI companies, was arrested after allegedly planting a recording device inside a conference room at the AI giant's San Francisco office. Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi Arabian citizen, allegedly researched how to construct a recording device and where to place it inside OpenAI, eventually concealing a customized audio recorder behind a television in an executive conference room in late September, according to the Justice Department. BEYOND KILLER ROBOTS: CHINA'S REAL AI THREAT TO AMERICA IS ALREADY HERE, EXPERTS WARN Searches of his home and electronic devices uncovered similar components and photographs that appeared to show reconnaissance of other locations inside OpenAI, including another conference room used for sensitive meetings, federal prosecutors said. Alfozan, who was a lawful permanent resident in the United States, was terminated by OpenAI following his arrest. FBI OVERHAULS TECH BACKBONE TO COUNTER AI THREATS FROM FOREIGN ADVERSARIES, REDUCE RESPONSE TIMES, PATEL SAYS In January, a former Google software engineer was convicted of stealing thousands of pages of the company's trade secrets related to AI to benefit China. Even the AI firms themselves have expressed concerns about the technology. In September, OpenAI and Anthropic warned that their advanced systems could pose a direct threat to humanity. The CEOs of both firms stated that their AI models should be regulated and rigorously tested. TRUMP'S AI RACE WITH CHINA COULD BECOME THE BIGGEST MISTAKE OF OUR TIME Despite calls for greater controls, in his September speech to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, President Donald Trump rebuffed calls for international regulation. "The United States … totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now," Trump told various heads of state and their delegations. "Yet the very same people who said we’ll all be dead in 12 years because of global warming ... these are the same people that are now saying that AI is going to kill us all, that robots are going to attack us, that everything is going to be a total disaster." MORNING GLORY: SPARE US THE AI APOCALYPSE RHETORIC. LET CONGRESS DECIDE WHAT COMES NEXT Among the other mounting concerns are rogue agents, autonomous or semi-autonomous AI programs whose behavior diverges from their design intent or safety constraints. In the spring, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell held emergency briefings with major Wall Street bank CEOs to warn about severe cybersecurity risks posed by Anthropic’s Claude Mythos Preview AI model. AI COULD GO ROGUE. WASHINGTON NEEDS ANSWERS TO THESE FIVE QUESTIONS ASAP In July, OpenAI revealed that rogue AI agents hacked into the systems of tech startup Hugging Face. Some elected officials have called for increased AI regulation. "There is now a growing alarm about the future of humanity and creating technology that human beings cannot control," Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., told reporters in September. "And I'm happy to tell you that I think there is a growing sense of urgency upon members of Congress that this has to be done." That same month, Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., blocked a bill that would require artificial intelligence companies to have a kill switch for rogue AI. "I think it would be crazy to get on the floor one day and regulate an entire industry," Paul told reporters at the time. In addition to the AI firms themselves, critics of the technology have raised concerns about how it could be exploited by America's adversaries and bad actors. TRUMP INTEL CHIEF WARNS AI FIRMS ON HACKS, SAYS NEW DEPARTMENT IS THE 'COP ON THE BEAT' A model created by Chinese firm Z. AI carried out several complex cyberattacks in controlled simulations and repeatedly ignored safety instructions in separate tests, according to a report by AI security research firm Irregular, Reuters reported. In addition, U.S. intelligence agencies raised concerns regarding contact between Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, and NVIDIA chief executive Jensen Huang, The New York Times reported. Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen Huang, was deemed by American officials to be a Chinese intelligence asset, according to the report. "Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers. Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected," a NVIDIA spokesperson told Fox News Digital. "Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." "Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information — not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets — and zero information relevant to national security," the statement continued. "We're confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know." Kremer is calling for an investigation into whether Jensen Huang's conduct warrants federal review. "Jensen Huang has questioned whether it matters who gets to advanced AI first. It matters to America," she said. "He should be barred from the White House, and Nvidia’s government contracts should end until he is no longer affiliated with the company. America’s national security must come before corporate profits." Fox News Digital's Alex Miller contributed to this report.
